ques: are there any differences between mixing with like those big machines people used to use versus mixing stuff in a daw... of course the process is different.. but i wonder if the actual sound ends up richer if you mix with those machines they used to use to mix like in the 90s or before... in fact 90s records tend to sound a lot more rich than modern records mixed digitally ... especially when it comes to rock stuff... im sure the way they did stuff was different back then... do you have any insight on this?
answ: not just in mixing, but most of the differences you're probably hearing are a result of people thinking about the whole thing differently based on what they can and cant do. for example, ever since 2000 something, you can make any note out of a singer's mouth perfectly in tune automatically. that's gonna have a big effect on the music. in the 90s it was very popular to sample things. so you get 4 bars of live-recorded drums from the 70s or something, stitched together every 4 bars. that creates a certain kind of 'looped' sound. but in the 1950s for example, you couldnt really do that. the drummer had to play the song all the way through. back then you couldnt even really edit, so everyone had to do everything all at once from beginning to end. there were fewer tracks on the machine (probably only 4) so you'd get whole bands playing the whole song through in 1 take. in the 1990s you probably dont get that as much. so in that sense, the 1990s is more modern than a time before. in the earliest days of recorded music, it was impossible to copy a record. so every record sold was a different recording of the song. the artist would be in the studio all day playing the song again and again and again, 1 for each copy of the record

If the song was recorded in another key and then pitch shifted to a new key (C), that might get kind of ugly, or it might actually sound cool with the pitch shift. If the song was written with KEY CHANGES but then was modified to keep it all in the same key but still have chord changes, within the key of C (C, F, G, Amin, Dmin, etc) then it's possible that the modified version could be worse, but it's also possible that it could be better. Then there's also a possibility that when you say "entirely in C major" you mean not just that the song is in that key but maybe you mean that every chord is C, or even more extreme, every note is C. like those viral pitch-correction experiments with 'hey now youre an allstar', or 'giant steps'. this could have some value just for being interesting, if you've never heard of that technology before. but then after the novelty wears off it wouldnt be so interesting. maybe the important thing which i should have said first, my entire answer here would be the same regardless of whether you were asking about C, Gb, or any key

ques: What's the first step you usually take when making a new song? do you start with improv, or memo down a tune that appears in your head, or something else?
answ: here is a general list of all the different ways, and i will try to explain the mechanics behind all of them. first we have to separate it into two general catagories: when it comes to me at a totally unexpected time and place, and when i do a dedicated session trying to get things to come to me on purpose now. When it drops on my head at an unexpected time, i immediately leap to write it down. usually a combination of a memo recording and text is best to convey all the necessary specifics of how it goes. if no harmonic musical instrument is available then i can explain the whole thing with just my voice, it just takes slightly longer to make sure i clarify and explain any harmonic information i might need. and if i absolutely cannot record a memo, then i have to get it done with text alone, in which case you see a lot of number charts, for melody, chords, AND rhythm, then me explaining it every different which way multiple times, just to make sure i'm clearly clarifying how it actually sounds. not so easy with text alone, but it can be done. so anyway that's how it works when the things come at me not on a writing session. But then there's when it's an actual writing session. now, you asked about the very first part of a song, so right now i am only talking about the starting sessions, which as i said include the unexpected drop-ins, and the deliberate session. but even with those deliberate sessions, right now i'm only referring to 'new idea' sessions, not the other types of sessions such as 'middle writing' (where i 'continue' writing on things) or production (which actually starts with 'selection' then writing to completion, then recording). So the 'new idea' sessions, deliberate sessions (not when it falls on my head at some other time), with those i usually do pretty high quantity just to get things going, and i make sure to spread it around a lot of different sorts of 'strategies'. things like, start with a tempo. or start with just a couple of words. or a keyboard improv. or a vocal improv. or a textual improv. sometimes i say i'm just gonna come up with 10 cool titles. sometimes i look at an image and see if that brings something. maybe browse maps, see if that brings up anything. It's often a bit bland to get the engine started on these new idea sessions at first, so it's important to have a little patience. i've learned over the years not to panic when the first few seem lousy. it can clearly be seen from the records of past sessions, that the first few are almost always pretty lame. which is an advantage as you get older, to be able to look back on past sessions and see how it all played out. Usually starts out like, ok that one sucked, do another one, ok well that one kinda almost didnt suck, but im not sure, then another one and another one and soon enough there is one where youre like "AH ok i THINK that one probably is good for something." then do another and another and you just kind of sort of lose track of how many youve done, and when you look back on it later you find that there are more good ones in there than you realized. so this is only the 'new idea' department that i've described here, both the deliberate session and catching the unnanounced drop-ins when off session

ques: would a hypothetical time signature of 7/7 be any different from 7/4? How would one count such a thing?
answ: no one denotes time signatures with the bottom number anything other than a power of 2 (1,2,4,8,16). the bottom number is ideally supposed to signify what the value of one beat is, as a fraction of 4/4. so for example, if the bottom number is 4, the quarter note gets one beat. if the bottom note is 8, an 8th note gets one beat. but these note values get their name for how they relate to 4/4. so if you want to say 7/7 then you have to figure out what a 7th note is. i suppose that would be like in 4/4 if you made a string of 8th notes with a polyrhythm indicator above them (such as 7:8, indicating "7 in the time where 8 would normally fit". so then you'd be imagining that 7 of those notes will fit in the bar. so then you've have to write "7:8" over every note you write, indicating that 7 of them would fit in the space where 8 would normally fit in 4/4, except now because we are in 7/7 you are declaring that only 7 of those fit in the bar. so the "8" and the polyrhythm notation would be totally redundant and it would be wasting a lot of writing on the page, and it would confuse any reader

ques: Bill,what inspires you to create songs about certain topics? why did you write mt saint helens is about to blow up to be about mount saint helens? how do you decide these things?

In the case of the song you mentioned, i can tell you how that happened. i was on a plane to portland, oregon, i saw a volcanic mountain out the window of the plane. i took a picture of it. then later, when i got to the hotel, in the room there was a picture of a big majestic volcanic mountain. it looked kind of like all those pictures of mount Fuji. somehow i jumped to multiple assumptions: that it's the same mountain i saw from the plane, that this mountain is like Portland's version of mount Fuji, a mountain that you can see from the city which everyone knows about. And somehow i also made the assumption that it was mount st helens. Later i've come to realize that perhaps all of these assumptions were wrong in multiple ways, but at the time i believed it. and in that moment, just a fraction of a second, i allowed myself to get curious about how a song about mount st helens might go. and the first 2 bars of the song flew into my head before i even had a chance to do it on purpose
